item.title: Residence permit B in Obvaldo: requirements and renewal
item.description: Permit B allows you to live and work in Switzerland on a renewable basis. Learn about the requirements, documents, and renewal procedure in the Obvaldo Canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit B: renewable document to live and work in Switzerland - Duration: from 1 to 5 years, with the possibility of renewal - Release: at the cantonal migration office - Requirements: employment contract, health insurance, good conduct
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit (category B) managed by SEM - When: Renewable before expiration (30-60 days in advance) - Where: Cantone Obvaldo - Who: Cantonal Office of Migration - Validity: Varies between 1-5 years, automatically renewable
The B residence permit is one of the main Swiss residence documents for foreigners who intend to reside and work in the federal territory. Unlike the C (domicile) permit, the B permit is renewable and is intended for those who have not yet accumulated enough years of residence to access a definitive status. In Canton Obvaldo, as in all Swiss cantons, the cantonal migration office is the authority responsible for the issuance, renewal and administrative management of the B permit.
### Key features of permit B
Permit B represents an intermediate category in the Swiss system of residence permits managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). This document allows the foreigner to live, work and settle in the territory of Switzerland for the duration of the permit. Its renewable nature distinguishes it from the L permit (of short duration, up to 1 ## # Residence Permit Requirements B
The B permit in the Obvaldo Canton follows federal criteria established by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), although the cantonal authority retains discretion in evaluating each application. The main requirements are:
1. ** Legitimate employment contract **: The foreigner must have an offer of employment confirmed by a Swiss employer. The contract must comply with Swiss working standards (maximum weekly duration, minimum holidays, etc.) and be compatible with the person's level of qualification. You can look for job opportunities in our [database di annunci](nav:jobs).
2. Certificate of Good Criminal Conduct: Issued by the country of origin, this document attests to the absence of serious criminal convictions. It must be recent (usually issued in the last 3-12 months).
3. Livelihood check: The salary agreed in the contract must be sufficient to cover the cost of living in the destination canton. There is no federal minimum wage, but each canton may have its own thresholds for wage acceptability.
4. Compulsory health insurance (LAMal/KVG): Within 3 months of arrival in Switzerland, the foreigner must take out a [assicurazione malattia](nav:health) with an authorized private provider. This insurance is required by law and premiums vary depending on the canton, region and deductible level chosen. Adult deductibles start from CHF 300 up to CHF 2,500 per year.
5. Documentation
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### B Permit Renewal Procedure
The renewal of the B permit is generally a simpler procedure compared to the initial application, as the cantonal office already has the applicant's personal, employment, and administrative data on file. However, it is essential to start the process well in advance to avoid any interruption in validity.
Step 1 — Check the expiration date: Verify the expiration date printed on your B permit. It is usually clearly highlighted.
Step 2 — Contact the cantonal office: Reach out to the cantonal migration office of the Canton of Obwalden at least 30-60 days before the expiration date. You can contact them by email, phone, or visit in person during their office hours.
Step 3 — Fill in the renewal form: The cantonal office will provide the specific renewal form. This form is generally also available online on the cantonal administration website. It is important to complete it fully and accurately.
Step 4 — Submit the documentation: Even though the documentation required for renewal is usually less burdensome than for the initial application, you will still need to submit a valid passport, an updated certificate of good conduct (if required), proof of valid health insurance (LAMal/KVG), and proof of your current employment situation or means of subsistence.
**Step 5 — Await approval**: The cantonal office will process the application. Processing times vary, but renewal is usually completed within 4-8 weeks. In case of delays, you can contact the office to check the status of your file.
### Cantonal Migration Office of the Canton of Obwalden
For the Canton of Obwalden, B permit applications and renewals must be submitted to the cantonal migration office (or equivalent name according to the local administrative organization). To obtain the exact office address, opening and reception hours, submission methods (online, by mail, at the counter, by appointment), specific cantonal administrative fees, and updated forms, we recommend consulting the official website of the Canton of Obwalden or contacting the cantonal administration directly.
### General Timelines and Costs
Processing times: The initial application usually takes 8-12 weeks (depending on the completeness of the documentation), while renewal is completed within 4-8 weeks. Administrative costs: Fees are set by each canton and may vary. Typically, renewal costs less than the initial application. For specific details on costs in the Canton of Obwalden, contact the cantonal migration office directly. Validity during the procedure: If you submit the renewal application before the expiration date, the validity of your permit is automatically extended until a decision is made on your application, even if the paper permit has technically expired.
### Next Steps
Once you have obtained your B permit, you can legally live and work in Switzerland for the period indicated on the document. If you intend to move to another canton, you must notify both your current cantonal office and the one of your new canton of residence of your change of address. Building a lasting career in Switzerland also requires conscious financial planning. Do the math: use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to check how federal, cantonal, and municipal tax rates affect your gross income. You can also fill in your [tax return](nav:tax-return) using the dedicated online tools, to better understand your tax situation once you have obtained your residence permit in the Canton of Obwalden.

item.title: Permit L in the Canton of St. Gallen: validity 12 months and extension rules
item.description: The short-term L permit in the Canton of St. Gallen has a maximum duration of 12 months, is linked to the employer and provides for extension only in exceptional cases. Here's how it works.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - L leave: duration up to 12 months, linked to a specific employer - Release from the Canton of St. Gallen for temporary missions of up to one year - Extension only in exceptional cases provided for by federal law - Passage to permit B linked to new application and contract beyond the year
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term L permit for foreign nationals with temporary employment in Switzerland - When: Maximum overall duration up to 12 months - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, issuing cantonal authority - Who: Cantonal Migration Authority of the Canton of St. Gallen, under the supervision of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Validity: linked to a specific employer and a specific activity - Extension: provided for only in exceptional circumstances by federal legislation - Transition: to residence permit B subject to new application and an employment relationship lasting more than one year
The short-term L permit is one of the residence permits provided for by Swiss federal legislation on foreigners. It is issued by the competent cantonal authorities — in the case of the Canton of St. Gallen by the cantonal office in charge — under the supervision of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). Its total maximum duration is set at twelve months, as established by the federal provisions on short-term permits applicable throughout Switzerland.
This residence permit is distinguished from the Obtaining an L permit in the Canton of St. Gallen means accepting a series of stringent constraints that clearly differentiate this title from the B permit. The most relevant is the link with the individual employer: those who change jobs during the validity of the permit must resubmit an application, with times and costs that start from scratch. The same applies to those who move from one activity to another, even within the same company.
### Maximum duration and extension: the actual margins
The total duration of the L leave may not exceed twelve months. The extension is allowed only in exceptional circumstances provided for by federal legislation: these are limited cases, usually linked to particular personal situations or to objective reasons that can be documented. In the practice of the Canton of St. Gallen — as in the rest of Switzerland — the granting of an extension is not automatic and requires a new investigation by the cantonal authority.
When the employment is extended beyond the year, it is not possible to extend the L permit: the change to a different title requires a new application. This step is technically distinct from the “extension” and is subject to different criteria, related to the nature of the new employment relationship.
### Moving to permit B: conditions and differences

To navigate the procedures for the L permit in the Canton of St. Gallen, it helps to follow an orderly path. The relevant cantonal office publishes the operational information and the required forms on its website; the documentation needed varies depending on nationality and the expected duration of the employment relationship.
### Step-by-step procedure
The first step is the submission of the application by the employer to the cantonal migration authority. The application must be accompanied by the signed employment contract, a description of the planned activity, the worker's identification details, and proof of accommodation. Once the application is received, the cantonal office checks that the admission conditions are met and, if applicable, forwards the file to the SEM for consultation.
After approval, the worker is called in for the collection of biometric data and the issuance of the permit. From that moment, the maximum twelve-month validity period begins.
### If the contract is nearing expiry
Before the contract expires, the worker and the employer must assess the situation. If the employment ends within the twelve months, the L permit expires automatically; staying in Switzerland is no longer permitted and the worker must leave the country, unless the worker has acquired the right to a different status.
If, on the other hand, the employment relationship continues beyond the year or turns into a permanent contract, the procedure for issuing a B permit begins. The application must be submitted before the L permit expires to avoid any interruption in the residence status.
### Documents and ancillary obligations
Once the L permit has been obtained, the worker must take care of several practical obligations: take out a LAMal health insurance policy within three months, register with the municipality of residence, open a bank account if necessary, and check registration with the AVS/AI/IPG and ALV/ALV-Z contribution scheme through the employer. The LPP applies from the moment the coordinated salary exceeds the entry threshold set by law.

item.title: Driving licence in the Canton of Svitto: procedure and examinations
item.description: How to obtain or convert your driver's license in the Canton of Schwyz: registration, theoretical and practical exams and compulsory courses according to federal regulations.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Obtaining a driving licence in Switzerland requires registration, theoretical and practical examination - Foreign license conversion follows uniform federal rules - Compulsory courses depend on the category and route of the applicant - The cantonal traffic office is the competent body for the application
## Key facts - **What**: driving licence procedure in the Canton of Schwyz, with a focus on conversion of foreign licences, examinations and compulsory courses - When: current regime (operational details to be verified at the cantonal office) - Where: Canton of Schwyz, competent traffic office - Who: Residents and persons intending to convert a foreign driver's license - How: registration with the cantonal authority, theoretical exam, practical exam, any courses - Reference: Federal Road Traffic Legislation (LCStr) and Admission to Traffic Ordinance (OAC)
Obtaining a driver's license in Switzerland means being subject to a federal regulatory framework applied by the cantons. In the Canton of Svitto, as in the rest of the country, the procedure involves the cantonal traffic office, a theoretical exam and a practical driving exam. The basic rules are set at national level by the Federal Law on Road Traffic and its ordinance, while the practical execution — from exam times to registration forms — is managed at cantonal level.

The procedure for obtaining or converting a driving licence in the Canton of Schwyz presents relevant practical differences depending on the applicant's starting point. Obtaining or converting a driving licence in the Canton of Schwyz requires following a precise sequence of steps. The procedure can be divided into distinct phases, each with specific documents and deadlines.
### Phase 1: Registration and documents
The first step is to go to the Canton's road traffic office (Strassenverkehrsamt) with the required documents: original driving licence (for conversion), valid identity document, passport-sized photograph, recent medical certificate, and proof of residence in a municipality of the canton. For an initial issuance, the original driving licence is not required.
### Phase 2: Examinations
For the conversion of a foreign driving licence, the practical exam must be taken with an examiner authorised by the canton. The theoretical exam may be required in addition, at the discretion of the cantonal authority and depending on the country of origin. Once the required exams have been passed and the cantonal fees have been paid, the office issues the Swiss driving licence. The document is normally valid for ten years and must be renewed with a new photograph upon expiry.
### Timelines and deadlines
Federal legislation provides that the foreign driving licence may be used in Switzerland for a transitional period after registering with the residents' registration office, but the conversion must be initiated within a set deadline. Once this deadline has passed, the foreign driving licence is no longer recognised for driving in Switzerland.

item.title: Wages and labour market Canton of Switzerland: sectors and levels
item.description: The labour market in the Canton of Schwyz: wage structure by degree of training, collective agreements, compulsory contributions and minimum rights.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - No federal minimum wage; some cantons set one by law - Wages vary by level of education (VET diploma, federal diploma, university degree) - OASI/IV contributions: 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - Collective labor agreements define pay standards by sector
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss wage structure by level of education and sector - OASI/IV contributions: 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - UI/ALV contributions: 1.1% up to an annual ceiling - Occupational pension (LPP/BVG): 7–18% according to age bracket (25–54+) - Health insurance (LAMal/KVG): mandatory for residents, per-capita premiums, not a payroll tax - Maximum working hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices) or 50 hours in other sectors
The labor market in the Canton of Schwyz follows the Swiss occupational structure, where wages are determined mainly by level of education, experience and sectoral collective agreements. Unlike many European countries, Switzerland does not set a federal minimum wage. Some cantons establish their own minimum wages through legislation, while others rely on sectoral collective agreements and market dynamics.
Education is the main driver of wage differentiation. Those who complete a vocational education and training (VET diploma of 3–4 years) gain access to technical and craft qualifications with higher pay than unskilled work. Those who obtain an advanced vocational diploma (federal diploma or federal examination) or a university degree access managerial and specialist roles with higher salaries.
### The contributions system on wages
In the Swiss pay system, the employee pays 5.3% of gross salary for OASI/IV (old-age and survivors' insurance and invalidity insurance) and EO/APG (loss-of-earnings compensation for maternity); the employer pays the matching 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. UI/ALV contributions (unemployment insurance) amount to 1.1% up to an annual ceiling. Accident insurance (UVG/LAA) ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the occupational sector. In addition, occupational pension provision (LPP/BVG) is mandatory for employees whose coordinated salary exceeds a threshold; contribution rates vary by age bracket: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ up to reference retirement age).
[Health insurance (LAMal/KVG)](nav:health) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and must be taken out within 3 months from the start of employment. It is not a payroll tax, but a private contract with per-capita premiums that vary by canton and region. Adults can choose annual deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500; higher premiums correspond to lower deductibles. ### Salary levels, training and collective contracts
The level of education remains the main differentiating factor in the Swiss labour market. Those who complete a vocational training (AFC) access typically higher salaries compared to unskilled work, with margins varying according to specialisation and market demand. Those who continue with higher education (federal diploma, federal examination, degree) access positions with greater responsibility and proportionally higher compensation.
Sectoral collective contracts (also called CCL or sectoral agreements) define minimum standards for salary, working hours and benefits for specific sectors: metallurgy, construction, commerce, pharmaceutical industry, advanced tertiary sector, and others. Even where there is no statutory cantonal minimum wage, collective contracts serve as an occupational reference and protect workers from compensation below certain levels.
### Working hours, holidays and minimum rights
Swiss law sets a maximum working time of 45 hours per week for industry, offices and sales; 50 hours for other sectors. Minimum holidays are 4 weeks per year (5 for those under 20). Maternity covers 14 weeks at 80% through loss-of-earnings compensation (IPG); paternity is 2 weeks. Notice periods for termination are: 1 month during the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards.
### Tax structure and pension provision
The Swiss tax system is structured on three levels: direct federal tax (IFD, uniform across the territory), cantonal taxes (varying by canton), and municipal taxes (applied as a multiplier on the cantonal rate). Canton Schwyz, like every canton, has its own cantonal tax rates and municipalities apply a local multiplier. The [occupational pension provision (LPP)](nav:pension) and the third pillar allow tax deductions for voluntary contributions, referring to federal and cantonal ordinances for details.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to navigate the Swiss labour market
For those seeking employment or negotiating a contract in Canton Schwyz, understanding how gross salary translates into net pay is essential. Many candidates do not correctly calculate the impact of mandatory insurance contributions on their actual take-home salary.
### Assessing gross salary and converting it to net
The first step is to gather salary benchmark data for your role, sector, and level of experience. If the employer adheres to a collective agreement, salaries are typically indexed to that scale. Online, bodies such as the FSO (Federal Statistical Office) and SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) publish median salary surveys by sector and canton.
Once you have identified a salary offer, it is essential to calculate the net amount: from gross salary you subtract AVS/AI contributions (5.3%), UI/ALV (1.1%), LAINF (0.7-1.5%), LPP (7-18% depending on age), and finally income taxes (federal, cantonal, municipal). A [salary calculator](nav:calculator) helps you visualise the net amount from a specific gross figure, including all contributions and taxes applicable in the canton.
### Choosing health insurance and reviewing the contract
Within 3 months of starting employment, the employee must take out a LAMal/KVG policy. Premiums vary significantly by canton and age bracket; choosing a higher deductible (up to CHF 2,500) reduces the monthly premium. Canton Schwyz offers premium subsidies for low-income earners, according to cantonal ordinances.
If the employer adheres to a collective agreement, request a copy of the applicable CLA (collective labour agreement), which specifies working hours, minimum wages, additional holidays, and benefits. If the proposed salary is below the collective agreement minimum, you have grounds to negotiate.
### Resources and next steps
To [search for specific job opportunities](nav:jobs) in the Swiss market, national platforms aggregate listings by sector and canton. Always calculate the net from the gross based on your personal and cantonal parameters using our [salary calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Army, the drone battalion is born: operational since 2028
item.description: Competence center presented to Thun by Pfister, Roos and Loher: reconnaissance and defense, plus a dedicated recruit school.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Army: a drone battalion operational since 2028 is born - Competence centre presented to Thun by Minister Pfister - A specific recruit school is planned to train the crews - Source reports an increase in drone overflights on sensitive sites
## Key facts - **What**: Presentation of the new drone competence centre and the future dedicated recruit school - When: Thursday, on the day of the presentation - Where: Place d 'art of Thun - Who: Defence Minister Martin Pfister, army chief Benedikt Roos, director of armasuisse Urs Loher - When operational: From 2028 the army will have the drone battalion - Battalion Mission: Reconnaissance and Defense - Function of the centre: Develop, experiment and integrate new technologies at the troop level
### The presentation to Thun Defence Minister Martin Pfister, army chief Benedikt Roos and Armasuisse director Urs Loher unveiled a new centre of expertise dedicated to drones, devices that are gaining increasing importance as tools of hybrid warfare, on the Thun parade ground on Thursday. The presentation took place at a time when even in Switzerland there is a phenomenon that makes us think: an increase in drone overflights over military infrastructure and sensitive installations.
### The skills of the new centre The centre will have the task of developing, testing and integrating these new technologies at the ## What changes for Switzerland
### Before and after the turning point Until now, the use of drones in the army has been entrusted to skills distributed across various units, without a dedicated centralized structure. With the new competence center and the future battalion, the training, equipment, and operational deployment of devices are brought together in a single national supply chain. For those living or working in Switzerland, this means a structural strengthening of a capability that directly concerns the defense of the country's airspace and critical infrastructure.
### Implications for national security The source emphasizes that drones are becoming increasingly important as instruments of hybrid warfare and that Switzerland is recording a rise in overflights above military infrastructure and sensitive installations. The creation of a specialized battalion responds precisely to this evolution: having trained personnel and systems tested at troop level allows for a more timely response to potential incursions or unauthorized reconnaissance activities. This is a significant step for the operational sovereignty of the Swiss army, which will be able to rely on a dedicated structure rather than on fragmented skills.
### Economic and industrial spillovers The competence center works alongside the activities of armasuisse, the federal office responsible for defense procurement and technological development. The development, testing, and integration of new technologies require investments in research, infrastructure, and qualified personnel, with effects that extend beyond military structures, involving suppliers and technology partners active in the Swiss market.
### The recruit school as an investment in human capital The creation of a recruit school dedicated to drones introduces a targeted training pathway capable of attracting profiles with specific technical skills. For young Swiss people interested in a career in the army, a new specialization opportunity opens up, with spillovers also into the civilian sector, where skills acquired on unmanned aerial systems are increasingly in demand.
### Scenario: what happens in case of unauthorized overflight The source notes an increase in overflights over sensitive infrastructure, without however providing details on specific episodes or any recent incidents. With a battalion operational from 2028, the army will have units trained both for reconnaissance and defense, reducing reaction times and standardizing intervention procedures compared to the current situation.
---

## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## What to know and how to get oriented
### Key timelines - **2025**: Official presentation of the competence centre at the Thun army training ground - 2028: Operational launch of the drone battalion for reconnaissance and defence - To be defined: Schedule of selections for the dedicated recruit school, not yet specified in the source
### Who manages the project The project involves three institutional levels: the Federal Department of Defence represented by minister Martin Pfister, the army command led by chief Benedikt Roos, and armasuisse, the federal defence procurement office headed by Urs Loher. Governance is therefore shared between political direction, operational command and technical-procurement responsibility.
### How the competence centre will work The centre will be tasked with developing, testing and integrating new technologies at troop level. In practice, this means that every new system or platform will go through a path that goes from research to operational use in the field, with the direct involvement of the units that will use the drones.
### Frequently asked questions about the new Swiss drone battalion For those who want to closely follow the evolution of the project, it is worth monitoring the communications of the Federal Department of Defence and armasuisse, which will publish updates on location, staffing and recruitment procedures.
### Scenario: how to prepare if you are interested in the sector For a Swiss citizen interested in working in the defence or technology sector, a hypothetical path could include: basic technical or engineering training, attention to tenders from armasuisse and the army for civilian and military positions, and — for young people of conscription age — the possibility of opting for the future recruit school dedicated to drones, as soon as the selection criteria are published.
### What to monitor in the coming months The source indicates 2028 as the year of operational capability of the battalion, but does not yet provide details on key aspects such as the number of personnel, the final location of the centre beyond the Thun army training ground, and the possible involvement of industrial partners. For now, the only certainty is that Switzerland is equipping itself with a national structure dedicated to drones, both for training and operational use.

item.title: Starting a business in the Canton of Schwyz: a practical guide
item.description: Complete procedure in the Canton of Schwyz: trade register, minimum capital for Sagl and SA, AVS, AD, LPP and LAMal obligations.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Opening a business in Switzerland requires registration in the cantonal trade register - The choice of legal form determines minimum capital and liability - Canton of Svitto: own tax laws and municipal multipliers - Insurance obligations (AVS, AD, LAINF, LPP) start from the first employee
## Key facts - **What**: procedure to start a business in the Canton of Schwyz - When: Fulfilments to be completed before the start of activities - Where: Canton of Schwyz, German-speaking Switzerland - Who: future entrepreneur, cantonal trade register, tax offices - Amount: minimum variable capital according to the legal form - Taxes: registration fees in the commercial register - Insurance: LAMal within 3 months, AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee, AD 1.1% - Pension: coordinated PPI for age groups 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55+
### Why Swivel The Canton of Swabia is one of the twelve jurisdictions of central Switzerland. Those who intend to open a business in this Canton must interface with the cantonal and municipal authorities for local taxation, while direct federal tax (DFT) and value added tax (VAT) follow federal law. Registration with the cantonal office of the trade register is the first formal step.
Svitto applies a cantonal tax law and a municipal multiplier that varies from one municipality to another, as is the case in the rest of Switzerland: each municipality multiplies the cantonal tax with a ### Registration and tax obligations After registration in the trade register, the new entrepreneur receives an IDI (business identification) number and is registered ex officio in the VAT and AVS registers. If the annual turnover exceeds the threshold of CHF 2,500 (taxable services), registration in the VAT register is mandatory. VAT registration is always mandatory for legal entities.
The IFD is a federal tax, managed by the AFC with progressive rates. Cantonal and municipal taxes are levied by cantonal tax administrations: in the case of Swift, by the Cantonal Tax Administration of the Swift Canton. The three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal) are summed up in the annual declaration.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure To open a business in the Canton of Schwyz, the aspiring entrepreneur must follow this procedure:
1. **Choice of legal form**: evaluate between sole proprietorship, GmbH (Sagl), AG (SA) or partnership, considering capital, liability and administrative costs.
2. Name and articles of association check: for GmbH and AG, a notarised deed of incorporation and articles of association are required, authenticated by a public notary. For GmbH, the minimum initial capital must be paid into a blocked bank account.
3. Entry in the commercial register: the application is submitted to the Commercial Register Office of the Canton of Schwyz (Handelsregisteramt). The articles of association, deed of incorporation, proof of capital payment and, for GmbH, bank confirmation are required. Cantonal registration fees vary; consult the official tariff schedule on the Canton's website.
4. VAT registration: with the Federal Tax Administration (FTA), if taxable turnover exceeds CHF 2,500 or for all legal entities.
5. Social fund registration: AHV compensation fund, unemployment fund, SUVA for accidents (mandatory from the first employee). Employers must affiliate with a compensation fund and pay contributions.
6. Health insurance (LAMal/KVG): every resident — owner and family members — must take out a basic policy within three months of arrival or start of business. Standard annual deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500.
7. Sector-specific authorisations: some activities (catering, healthcare, construction, transport) require additional cantonal or federal permits.
### Deadlines and obligations After starting up, the entrepreneur must: - pay VAT advances quarterly (or monthly above a certain threshold); - file federal, cantonal and municipal tax returns every year; - pay salary contributions within the deadlines set by the compensation funds; - keep accounts in accordance with the Code of Obligations and Swiss GAAP FER standards where applicable.

## In a nutshell - Registration in the Commercial Register is mandatory before starting business - Minimum capital ranges from CHF 0 (sole proprietorships) to CHF 100,000 (SA) - Registration fees vary by canton and legal form - Compulsory social contributions for employees: 10.6% AVS/AI/IPG with employer
## Key facts - **What**: Registration in the Commercial Register in the Canton of Schwyz - When: Before the start of business - Where: Office of the Registrar of Commerce of the Canton of Schwyz - Who: Entrepreneurs, sole proprietorships, companies - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship, Sagl, SA - Minimum capital Sagl: CHF 20,000 - SA Minimum Capital: CHF 100,000 - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 10.6% total (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer)
The Canton of Swabia, like all Swiss cantons, requires compulsory registration in the Commercial Register for anyone intending to start a business. This procedure is the first administrative step and represents a crucial moment in the startup phase of any company. Before starting business operations, entrepreneurs and company owners must complete registration with the competent cantonal office, which varies depending on the legal form chosen.
The choice of legal form is decisive not only for organisational aspects, but also for financial and tax burdens. In the canton of Switzerland, as in the whole of Switzerland, there are several options: from the sole proprietorship (self-management) to the ### Three-tier tax system
In the Canton of Schwyz, as throughout Switzerland, the tax system operates on three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. Each level has its own legislation and tax rate.
Direct Federal Tax (DFD) is administered by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA) and represents the federal level. Cantonal tax is managed by the cantonal authorities of Schwyz and is calculated according to its own cantonal law. Finally, municipalities apply a multiplier to the cantonal base, which means that local taxation varies depending on the company's domicile.
This three-tier structure requires the entrepreneur to consider not only the federal rate, but also the specific cantonal and municipal rates. This configuration is not found in many countries, where the tax system is centralized at one or two levels. To plan tax aspects, consult the federal tax calculator.
### Insurance obligations for employees
If the business involves hiring employees, significant insurance obligations arise immediately. Under Swiss labor law, the employer is required to pay social contributions for each employee.
⚠️ OASI (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance), DI (Disability Insurance), and EO (Income Compensation Allowance) contributions represent 5.3% of the employee's salary, to which an identical contribution from the employer is added, for a total of 10.6%. These contributions finance the first pillar of the Swiss pension system.
Accident insurance (UVG/LAA) is mandatory for employees working on a primary basis and varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity. This amount is borne by the employer.
For employees with an income of CHF 22,050 and above, the employer must also make payments for the second pension pillar (BVG/LPP), with rates that vary according to age: 7% between 25 and 34 years, 10% between 35 and 44 years, 15% between 45 and 54 years, and 18% from 55 years of age up to the reference age. To learn more about the second pillar, consult the [OASI/BVG guide](nav:pension).
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and must be taken out within 3 months of arrival. For employees, the cost depends on the cantonal premium (which varies by canton and region) and does not represent a direct cost for the employer, but is borne by the employee.
These charges represent a significant cost item in personnel management and must be considered in the startup budget. Their correct management is crucial for the success of the business.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure
To start a business in the Canton of Schwyz, following these steps is essential:
**1. Choose the legal form** Before taking any other action, define the type of enterprise. Consult an accountant or a lawyer specialized in commercial law to choose the structure that best suits your needs. Remember that the minimum capital varies: zero for sole proprietorships, CHF 20,000 for LLCs (Sagl), CHF 100,000 for corporations (SA).
2. Prepare the documentation Depending on the legal form, gather the necessary documents: Commercial Register extracts from previous experiences, identity documents of the owners, company statutes (for corporations), deed of incorporation, and bank certificates of capital deposit (for LLCs and SAs).
3. Register with the cantonal Commercial Register Contact the Commercial Register office of the Canton of Schwyz with the prepared documentation. Registration takes place at the competent cantonal authority and marks the official start of business activity.
4. Apply for the federal VAT number If the expected annual turnover exceeds CHF 100,000, you must register for VAT with the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV). This number is necessary to issue invoices and manage federal tax obligations.
5. Register for cantonal and municipal taxes Contact the tax office of the Canton of Schwyz to register for cantonal and municipal taxes. You will receive details on deadlines, rates, and specific payment procedures.
6. Start social security contributions If you will be hiring employees, register with the competent OASI (AVS) Compensation Fund for the payment of social security contributions. Contact an insurance company for mandatory accident insurance.
7. Take out health insurance for employees Remember that every employee must have mandatory health insurance within 3 months of the start date. This is not the employer's direct duty, but ensure that your employees are covered.
### Important deadlines
Commercial Register registration must take place before the start of business. VAT registration, if necessary, has deadlines defined by the FTA. Social security contributions must begin from the month the first employee is hired. Annual tax returns have federal and cantonal deadlines that vary — your accountant will guide you on these.
### Useful tools
To manage the financial aspects of your business and understand personnel costs, use the [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) to evaluate the tax and social security burden of your employees.
Starting a business in the Canton of Schwyz follows the same procedures as the rest of Switzerland. The process is well-regulated and each cantonal office can provide assistance. The key is to plan ahead and obtain good business advice.

## Key facts - **What**: Start-up of a self-employed or corporate activity in the Canton of Schwyz - When: the source does not indicate a specific date; the procedure is permanent - Where: Canton of Schwyz, central Switzerland - Who: future entrepreneur, cantonal trade register, tax authorities - Amount: minimum capital variable according to the legal form (the source does not specify amounts) - Tax authorities: AFC/ESTV for IFD and VAT; cantonal administrations for cantonal and municipal taxes - Pension: UFAS/BSV for AVS, AI and LPP - Health insurance: mandatory within 3 months of arrival or start of activity
Starting a business in the Canton of Swiss requires compliance with a series of requirements that cross federal and cantonal law. The first step is to choose the legal form, which determines the minimum capital, the corporate structure and the degree of personal responsibility.
In Switzerland the most common legal forms are the individual activity, the partnership (Kollektivgesellschaft according to the German denomination), the limited partnership (Kommanditgesellschaft), the ### Capital, responsibility and strategic choice
The choice of legal form is not just a bureaucratic matter: it affects property liability, the ability to raise capital and the tax burden. An individual activity does not require minimum capital but exposes the holder to unlimited liability. The Kollektivgesellschaft (joint venture) operates with at least two shareholders who are jointly and severally liable; the Kommanditgesellschaft instead provides for at least one general partner, whose liability is limited to the contribution.
Särl/Sàrl and AG/SA are joint-stock companies: liability is limited to the capital contributed. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure for starting a business

2. Check the availability of the name. Before registration, you must ensure that the chosen name is not already registered. The search service is available at the commercial register office.
3. Draft the founding deed and articles of association. For GmbH/Sàrl and AG/SA a public deed is required; for partnerships, a written contract between the partners may suffice.
4. Pay in the minimum capital and open a bank account. The payment must be certified by the bank and the amount deposited in the business account.
5. Register with the commercial register. The application is submitted to the cantonal office, with all required documents. The source notes the existence of registration fees, but the specific amount is not indicated: to be requested directly from the office.
6. Register with the tax authorities. Distinguish between direct federal tax/VAT (FTA/ESTV) and cantonal/municipal taxes (tax administration of Canton Schwyz). The source clarifies the respective competences: the FTA/ESTV handles direct federal tax and VAT, cantonal administrations handle the rest.
7. Register with a compensation fund. For OASI/DI/IC contributions and, if you hire employees, also unemployment insurance and LAINF (occupational accident insurance).
8. Take out the mandatory insurances. LAMal (health insurance) within 3 months of starting the activity for the owner and family members; LAINF for employees.
### Deadlines and recurring obligations
- VAT return: usually quarterly, with rates defined by the FTA. - Tax return: annual, with cantonal deadlines. - Payment of social security contributions: monthly or quarterly depending on the compensation fund.

item.title: Buying a Svitto home: prices and mortgage
item.description: Practical guide: acquiring a property in the canton of Schwyz requires own funds, a sustainable mortgage, a transfer tax and notary fees. Complete procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Purchasing a home in the canton of Schwyz requires own funds and a sustainable mortgage. - The property transfer tax is a cantonal levy applied to real estate transactions. - Notary fees and registration in the land register are additional components of the total cost.
## Key facts
- **What**: Purchase of a home in the canton of Schwyz with assessment of prices, mortgage, own funds and taxes. - When: Procedure ranging from a few months (search) to a few weeks after the offer. - Where: Canton of Schwyz (Central Switzerland). - Who: Prospective buyers (residents, investors, foreigners with permits). - Amount: Variable depending on the property price, cantonal property transfer tax rate, and notary fees.
Those who decide to buy a house in the canton of Schwyz face an articulated procedure that touches on numerous aspects: from the assessment of market prices to the gathering of own funds, from the sustainability of the mortgage to the calculation of taxes and notary fees. The Canton of Schwyz, like every Swiss canton, applies its own tax rules and regulations that influence the final cost of the investment.
Purchasing a property is a significant financial decision, not only for the purchase price, but also for the initial capital outlay (own funds), the annual expenses (mortgage instalment, property taxes, insurance) and the one-off costs linked to the transfer of ownership (property transfer tax, notary fees, land register registration).
### Determining factors in the Schwyz real estate market
The value of properties in the Canton of Schwyz varies according to concrete factors: geographical location (proximity to main municipalities, accessibility by public transport), property characteristics (size, year of construction, state of maintenance) and the local economic context. At national level, the Swiss real estate market is monitored by federal statistical offices (FSO/BFS) and cantonal administrations, which publish periodic data on price trends.
You can consult the data on the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) to assess the overall sustainability of the property investment within the Swiss economic context. The mortgage is the fundamental tool for financing the purchase: Swiss banks offer tailored solutions, but they require solid guarantees in terms of own funds paid directly by the borrower. The sustainability of the monthly instalment is assessed by each institution according to shared federal criteria, with a prudential view of risk.
### The role of the mortgage in the transaction
The mortgage is not only a financing tool, but it directly affects the sustainability of the investment in the medium and long term. Banks require the borrower to demonstrate sufficient repayment capacity and to pay part of the price as own funds. This structure balances the risk between the lending institution and the buyer, protecting them from insolvency scenarios or fluctuations in the real estate market. ### Mortgage sustainability: criteria and assessment
Once the property has been identified and the purchase price defined, the next step is to verify whether the proposed mortgage is actually sustainable over time. Swiss banks apply strict criteria: the monthly instalment (principal + interest + insurance) must not exceed 30-35% of the household's gross monthly income. This ratio is called the 'debt-to-income ratio' (DTI) and varies slightly from one institution to another, but follows a logic of federal prudential soundness.
Even more cautious is the practice of the 'stress test': banks simulate a future scenario in which the interest rate rises by one or two percentage points compared to the current rate and verify that the instalment remains sustainable. If a scenario with higher rates were to make the instalment unsustainable, the mortgage amount is reduced. This mechanism protects the borrower in the event of future rate increases.
In addition to the main income, banks assess other financial obligations of the borrower: credit cards with active balances, car leases, personal loans. If the borrower has substantial payment obligations, the available mortgage capacity decreases. This integrated view of the credit profile reduces the risk of insolvency over time.
### Own funds: percentages and accumulation strategies
Swiss banks do not finance 100% of the purchase price. As a rule, the borrower must contribute at least 20% as own funds. This percentage acts as a safeguard: if the property value drops and the borrower can no longer repay the mortgage, the bank retains a margin of security in the value of the property.
Some institutions accept lower own funds (from 10% to 15%), but in that case they often require a mortgage credit insurance (LLM insurance) which the borrower must pay, increasing the total cost of the financing. Accumulating own funds takes time: many buyers build them up through private savings, inheritances, the sale of previous properties, or pension contributions (for example, a partial withdrawal from a private pension account [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3), where permitted by federal law and the institution's rules).
### Comparative scenarios: 70% vs. 80% vs. 90% mortgage
To illustrate the impact of own funds on sustainability, let's consider three hypothetical scenarios where the price is fixed, but the percentage of own funds varies. With the same interest rate and borrower's income, a mortgage financing 90% of the value (10% own funds) is more burdensome in terms of monthly instalment and carries the risk of additional insurance. A mortgage at 70-80% (20-30% own funds) reduces the monthly instalment and often does not require insurance, making the investment more sustainable in the medium to long term. This flexibility allows the borrower to tailor the financing to their own risk profile and financial resources.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure: from interest to the purchase deed
Step 1: Research and preliminary evaluation. The first step is to identify properties of interest in the Canton of Schwyz and request a preliminary assessment from banks or wealth managers. At this stage, the potential buyer provides information on income, assets, and available equity. The bank provides a (non-binding) indication of the mortgage amount that could be granted.
**Step 2: Offer and negotiation.** Once the desired property has been found, the buyer submits an offer to the seller. Negotiations may concern the price, handover date, and maintenance work. During this phase, it is advisable to request a formal property valuation from a bank appraiser.
Step 3: Formal mortgage application. Once the offer is defined, the borrower submits a formal mortgage application to the bank, attaching documentation: bank statements, tax returns, the offer letter, and the property valuation. The bank carries out a detailed credit analysis and communicates the amount it can grant and the terms (rate, duration, monthly instalment).
Step 4: Notary and deed of sale. Once the mortgage is confirmed, the parties turn to a notary. In the Canton of Schwyz, the notary draws up the deed of sale (rogito), which must comply with the formalities required by cantonal law. The deed describes the property, the contracting parties, the price, the conditions of transfer, and the incidence of the transfer tax.
Step 5: Disbursement of funds and registration. Before the final signature, the borrower pays in the agreed equity. At the same time, the bank subscribes the mortgage loan and registers it with the cantonal land registry (Grundbuch), obtaining a mortgage lien on the property. The entry in the land registry is managed by the competent office of the Canton of Schwyz.
Step 6: Transfer of ownership. Upon signing of the notarial deed, ownership is transferred from the seller to the buyer. The transfer tax is calculated and paid according to the procedures set out by Swiss cantonal law.
### Transfer tax and notary fees: components of the final cost
The transfer tax is a cantonal levy that applies to the transfer of ownership of a property. Each Swiss canton sets its own rates and rules: the Canton of Schwyz, like other central cantons, applies this tax according to specific laws and regulations. The amount depends on the value of the property at the time of transfer. Exemptions are often provided for transfers between spouses, direct descendants, or ascendants; the exact conditions vary by canton and require verification with the notary.
Notary fees cover the drafting of the deed, authentication, and the administrative handling of the sale. These fees are set by cantonal tariffs and typically amount to 1–2% of the property value, depending on the complexity of the transaction.
Additional costs include the registration in the land registry (cantonal office fees) and any costs for an appraiser or real estate agency. Together, these additional charges usually amount to 3–5% of the purchase price.
📊 For a complete and personalised estimate, the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate the costs related to the purchase and check the impact on financial sustainability. To learn more about federal and cantonal taxation rules, see the dedicated guide on tax obligations and deductions for property owners.

item.title: Buying a house in Svitto: prices, mortgage and own funds
item.description: Complete guide to buying a house in Svitto: own funds required, mortgage loan, transfer taxes, notary fees and legal procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Own funds required: 20-30% of the purchase price - Mortgage loan: main financing method for the remaining 70-80% - Transfer taxes: vary by canton (0-3.6% in Switzerland) - Notarial procedures and property registration: mandatory, vary by canton
## Key facts - **What is required**: Own funds (20-30%), mortgage loan (70-80% of the price) - Where to buy: In Canton Schwyz and in other Swiss cantons - Who is involved: Buyer, bank (financing), notary, land registry office - Ancillary costs amount: Transfer taxes (cantonal), notary fees (0.3-1.2%), registration charges - Procedure: Approximately 6-12 months from initial search to property transfer
Buying a house in Switzerland is one of the most significant steps in the life of a resident. Whether you are purchasing in Canton Schwyz or in any other canton, the process follows well-defined federal and cantonal rules. The main challenge for many buyers is not finding the right house, but arranging financing: Swiss banks generally require the buyer to have own funds equivalent to 20-30% of the purchase price. The remaining 70-80% is financed through a mortgage loan, a loan secured by the property itself.
### Financing: own funds and mortgage loan
The real estate financing system in Switzerland is based on a clear division between own capital and loan. If a house costs CHF 500,000, the bank expects you to have at least CHF 100,000-150,000 to put on the table. The mortgage loan covers the rest. This model protects both the bank (whose loan is secured by the property) and the buyer (who will not over-indebt themselves).
The sustainability of the mortgage is crucial. Swiss banks use conservative calculations: they verify that the monthly installment does not exceed a fixed percentage of your net income (generally 33%). A further assessment concerns the value of the property itself — the mortgage cannot exceed 80-90% of that value according to the independent bank appraisal.
### Property taxes and charges
When you buy a house, taxes apply at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. The federal direct tax (FTT/IFD) is withheld by the employer and does not apply directly to the purchase price. However, the transfer of ownership of a property is subject to the transfer tax — a cantonal tax that varies considerably between cantons. In some Swiss cantons it is almost non-existent, in others it reaches 3-3.6% of the sale price. This rate benefits the canton and the municipalities where the property is located.
In addition to the transfer tax, you will need to pay notary fees and registration charges at the Land Registry (Grundbuch). The notary drafts the purchase contract in accordance with cantonal law, has it signed by both parties in front of witnesses (or certifying the signatures if signed elsewhere), and transmits the document to the Land Registry. Notary fees vary between cantons (typically 0.3-1.2% of the price), as do registration charges.
According to the Federal Statistical Office (FSO/BFS), prices of residential properties vary significantly between Swiss cantons, affecting the local cost of living. If you intend to purchase a property, consider that VAT on the construction of a new house also applies (7.7% on the value of the work).
[Use our mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate how much you can borrow based on your own funds. ## Local taxes and cantonal variability
The transfer tax is the most significant 'hidden' cost of buying real estate in Switzerland. The law governing it is cantonal, not federal. This means that the canton where the property is located sets the rate, and the tax burden can differ drastically between neighbors.
### Variable rates across cantons
In the canton of Schwyz, as in other cantons, the transfer tax rate is set by cantonal legislation. In Switzerland, rates range from 0% (some cantons) up to 3.6% (cantons with high tax pressure). A property of 600,000 CHF would result in a transfer tax between 0 CHF and 21,600 CHF depending on the canton — an enormous difference that influences the purchasing decision.
In addition to the transfer tax, municipalities have the option of levying annual taxes on real estate ownership. These taxes are much smaller (generally 0.05-0.3% of the assessed value annually) but should be considered in long-term budgets.
### Notary fees and land registration
Notary fees are not a tax, but a charge for the legal certification service and drafting of the contract. They vary considerably by canton: - Cantons with regulated rates: 0.3-0.7% of the price - Cantons with free rates: can reach up to 1.2% - Land registration at the Grundbuch: 10-100 CHF (one-time administrative charge)
A buyer purchasing for 500,000 CHF therefore pays: - Notary fees: 1,500-6,000 CHF - Land registration: 10-100 CHF - Transfer tax (if applicable in Schwyz): 0-18,000 CHF (example with a 3.6% rate) - Total ancillary costs: 1,500-24,000 CHF
This is not a negligible sum. For this reason, it is advisable to contact a notary in the area where you intend to buy — many notaries provide preliminary cost estimates free of charge.
### Federal tax aspect: withholding tax on gains
If you sell a house after just a few years (especially if it has appreciated in value), the gains may be subject to real estate capital gains tax. This tax is federal, cantonal, and municipal, and rates vary enormously between cantons. Buying to live in (primary residence) is generally favorable from a tax standpoint compared to buying as a real estate investment.
[Consult our guide to the tax return](nav:tax-return) to understand the tax implications of buying and selling property, and explore the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to frame property prices within the general economic context.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to buy a house in Switzerland: step-by-step procedure
Buying a house is not immediate. Here are the main steps that almost all buyers go through.
Start with an honest assessment of your financial capacity. Approach a bank and request a Hypothekarfähigkeitsbestätigung (mortgage eligibility declaration in German) — a document that certifies how much the bank is willing to lend you. This is not yet a mortgage, but a preliminary assessment that provides a realistic budget limit.
Once you know your budget, you can start looking for the house. In Switzerland, properties are found through online real estate portals, real estate agents, or local listings in newspapers. When you find an interesting property, the agent (or the seller) requires a written offer. This offer is not legally binding at this stage, but it shows the seriousness of your interest and starts price negotiations.
### Step 4-6: Mortgage and technical inspection
After your offer is accepted, formally apply for the mortgage at the bank. The bank orders a technical appraisal of the property to verify that its value justifies the requested loan. Once the mortgage is approved (a process that can take 2-4 weeks), you are authorized to proceed with the purchase agreement.
At the same time, it is highly advisable to have the house inspected by an independent technical expert. Although not required by law, an inspection reveals structural problems (dampness, foundations, roof, systems) that could cost thousands of CHF in the future.
### Step 7-8: Notarial contract and land registry registration
When everything is ready (mortgage approved, inspection completed, price terms agreed), the sale goes to the notary. The notary drafts the purchase agreement in accordance with cantonal law, has both parties sign it in front of witnesses, and transmits the document to the Land Registry.
The Land Registry (Grundbuch) is the public register of real estate ownership, managed at cantonal level. Once the contract is registered, the property legally passes to you. This step concludes the official transfer of ownership.

In the Canton of Uri, as in every other canton, the municipal tax is calculated using a multiplier applied to the cantonal tax. In the Swiss three-column system, the first pillar — Old Age and Survivors Insurance (AVS/AHV) — is the basis of compulsory social security for those residing or working in Switzerland. Each canton has its own cantonal compensation fund that acts as an operational counter for workers, employers, pension recipients and claimants of supplementary benefits. In the canton of Uri, the cantonal compensation fund is the entity designated to receive wage declarations, collect AVS/AI/IPG contributions and manage applications for ## How supplementary benefits work in the Canton of Uri
Supplementary benefits (SB) to OASI/DI are regulated at the federal level by the Supplementary Benefits Act (LPC), but their payment and operational management is entrusted to the cantons. In Uri, responsibility lies with the cantonal compensation fund in collaboration with the social services, which process the application, collect the documents and calculate the monthly amount due.
### The calculation formula
The SB amount is given by the difference between recognised expenses and computable income. Recognised expenses include the amount for basic needs (distinguished for single persons, couples, families), the actual rent (up to a recognised maximum), medical and paramedical expenses not covered by other insurances, and other items provided for by the LPC. Computable income, on the other hand, consists of the OASI/DI pension, any income from work, income from assets (assets above an exemption threshold are converted into notional income), third-party benefits and family allowances. If the difference is positive, the applicant is entitled to SB for the corresponding amount.
### Who is entitled to SB
Persons who receive an OASI or DI pension, or who — within a certain time horizon — would be entitled to a pension, are entitled to SB, provided their economic situation meets the legal criteria. The application may also be submitted by persons who have not yet reached the reference age, if they receive a DI pension. For recipients of modest pensions, SB is often the difference between a poor old age and a dignified old age: in many situations the OASI pension alone does not even cover the rent and basic expenses.
### Hypothetical scenario: a couple with a minimum pension
Consider a couple residing in Uri in which both have paid full contributions but with always low-to-medium incomes, receiving two reduced OASI pensions and living in a rented apartment. If the recognised expenses (basic needs for a couple, actual rent, health insurance premiums) exceed the sum of the OASI pensions and other income, the difference is covered by the SB, paid monthly by the compensation fund. The same person, with a small additional income from a reduced gainful activity, would see the SB amount reduced but not necessarily the entitlement cancelled.
### Implications for the family budget
Obtaining SB means for many elderly people being able to stay in their own home, pay health insurance premiums (LAMal) and maintain a minimum standard of living. The SB is recalculated annually, and the beneficiary is required to communicate any change in income, assets or housing situation. In Uri, as in the rest of Switzerland, SB applications are growing structurally, linked both to the increase in housing costs and to the share of reduced pensions for careers with low incomes or contribution interruptions.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Practical procedure: how to submit your application in Uri
Obtaining the AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance) pension and, if necessary, supplementary benefits (PC) in the Canton of Uri requires a few precise steps. The procedure is defined at the federal level, but the point of contact is the cantonal compensation office of Uri (Ausgleichskasse Uri).
### Step 1 — Check your contribution record
Before submitting any application, it is useful to request an extract of the individual account (CI) from the FSIO (UFAS/BSV) or through the compensation office. The individual account lists all contributions paid, recorded income, and any gaps. If missing years appear, discuss with the compensation office the possibility of a retroactive payment.
### Step 2 — Applying for the AVS pension
The AVS pension is not paid automatically: it must be requested from the Uri compensation office, usually a few months before reaching the reference age. The office sends the forms, collects the required documents (family record, salary certificates, any periods of work abroad) and forwards the file for calculation. The first pension is normally paid retroactively from the month of application, not earlier.
### Step 3 — Possible application for supplementary benefits (PC)
If the AVS pension — alone or together with other income — does not cover the vital minimum needs, the PC phase opens. The application is submitted to the Uri compensation office with the following typical documents: AVS/AI pension decision, rent certificate and lease agreement, bank and securities statements, insurance policies (life, 3a), and spouse's income certificates. The office checks the recognised expenses and computable income and issues the decision.
### Step 4 — Reporting changes
Every relevant change — rent change, inheritance, sale of property, start of a gainful activity, death of a spouse — must be reported to the compensation office within the set deadlines. Failure to report may lead to a reduction or revocation of the PC, with recovery of amounts already paid.
### Timelines and deadlines
Decision times vary depending on the complexity of the case: a simple AVS application can be processed in a few months, while a PC file with complex documentation may take longer. It is advisable to submit the PC application immediately after the pension starts, to avoid income gaps. Specific deadlines apply to applications for retroactive payment of missing contributions, to be checked case by case with the compensation office.
### Where to get information
For any information on AVS and PC in the Canton of Uri, the first point of contact is the cantonal compensation office of Uri (Ausgleichskasse Uri). The canton's official website provides the address, opening hours and downloadable forms.

item.title: Graubünden: guaranteed cash payment for services
item.description: The Grand Council approves the Bettinaglio counter-project: taxes and transport in Graubünden can be paid in cash, despite digitalisation.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Guaranteed cash payment for taxes and public services in Graubünden. - The Bettinaglio counter-project approved with 83 votes in favor. - The popular initiative has already collected over 16,000 signatures in the Canton. - Exceptions provided for security reasons or technical impossibility.
## Key facts - **What**: Parliamentary resolution for the use of cash in public services - When: Grand Council decision of November 13, 2024 - Where: Canton of Graubünden (Chur) - Who: Graubünden Grand Council, SVP, Martin Bettinaglio (The Centre) - Amount: 16,000 signatures collected (4,000 quorum required)
The Grand Council of Graubünden has established a principle that directly affects the daily lives of residents and taxpayers: the possibility of paying in cash for cantonal and municipal taxes, as well as for the use of public infrastructure, must be guaranteed. The decision, reached today in the chamber, represents a regulatory anticipation of what is requested by a popular initiative currently following its path towards a vote. The parliamentary debate concluded with a clear majority in favor of the counter-project presented by Grand Councilor Martin Bettinaglio, a representative of The Centre, which received 83 votes in favor, compared to 30 against and four abstentions.
### Political genesis and the compromise in the chamber The issue was initially raised by a motion from the SVP, which called for strong protections for the use of physical money in dealings with the public administration. The original text was however softened through Bettinaglio's counter-project, which sought a balance between the citizen's freedom of choice and the operational needs of the offices. Even the SVP itself agreed to mitigate its initial demands in order to see the core principle approved in the cantonal legislature. However, some gray areas remain, as pointed out by the FDP, which voted against the proposal. The Liberals highlighted a potential overlap with the popular initiative of the same name, which, proceeding in parallel, risks creating a dual regulatory track. Furthermore, the 'reasonableness' clause was criticized, deemed too vague to precisely define when a public body can legitimately refuse banknotes. This decision will influence how citizens interact with [public transport](nav:transport) and municipal counters, reinforcing the role of cash in an era of push towards the digitalization of payments. ### The popular initiative and the case of direct sales The political ferment surrounding physical money in Grisons did not emerge in a vacuum, but is the result of a significant popular mobilization called 'Cash payment of public services', also defined by its promoters as the 'Initiative against discrimination'. The committee, led by retiree Berta Caminada, gave voice to a widespread discontent resulting from operational decisions made by entities such as PostBus and the Department of Infrastructure, Energy and Mobility. The spark was the abolition of direct cash ticket sales by onboard staff on buses, a measure that prompted Caminada to first launch a petition, which gathered 8,000 signatures, and then the initiative itself.
The numbers from the signature collection, cited during the debate by the president of the SVP parliamentary group Stefan Metzger, describe massive support: since June, over 16,000 signatures have been filed, a figure four times higher than the 4,000 required to bring the issue to a popular vote. The orientation of the initiative is very similar to that of the counter-project just approved by Parliament, calling for cash to remain a valid means of payment for taxes, public parking, and even access to public toilets. It is essential to note that the obligation to accept would not be extended to private sector companies, limiting the scope of action only to public or state-co-financed companies. This aspect is crucial for those who must evaluate their [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) and daily expense management methods in the Canton, as it guarantees a plurality of options for mandatory payments to the public entity.
### Exceptions to the cash rule Despite the general principle being established, the resolution provides for specific safeguard clauses. Cash payment may be limited or excluded if the offer is not reasonable or appropriate for prevailing reasons. These include the safety of operators, protection against possible abuse, and technical impossibility. This last point particularly concerns automated systems that are not designed to handle coins or banknotes and whose adaptation would involve disproportionate costs. The debate now shifts to the practical application of these concepts: what is meant by 'reasonable' remains the most debated point, with the risk that the discretion of individual offices could limit the effectiveness of the new rule.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Procedures and impact for residents For citizens residing in Grisons, the Grand Council's resolution opens a transitional phase in the management of financial relations with the State. Once implemented, the legislation will allow visiting municipal or cantonal counters to pay taxes without necessarily having credit cards or banking applications. The procedure for paying taxes, which usually occurs via payment slips, must therefore maintain channels that allow the use of cash, facilitating segments of the population less accustomed to technology or those who prefer not to digitally track every transaction. Also for the use of infrastructure, such as public parking, municipalities will have to evaluate whether current systems respect the criterion of reasonableness in accepting physical money.
The next steps include: - Integration of the cash principle into cantonal and municipal legal bases. - Technical evaluation of ticket vending machines for [public transport](nav:transport) and parking meters. - Possible popular vote on the initiative, should the promoters decide not to withdraw it despite the approval of the counter-project.
Those living or working in the Canton must consider that, although the public sector is moving towards this protection of cash, private transactions remain regulated by contractual freedom. Therefore, for expenses related to rent or purchases at commercial establishments, payment methods will continue to be established by individual providers. The Swiss hospitality sector recorded 3.9 million overnight stays in the second quarter of thisyear, a slight increase of 0.4% compared to the same period in 2025. This is reported today by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), in a framework that confirms domestic demand as the main driver of statistics.
### The three sectors in detail Holiday homes contributed 1.0 million overnight stays, down 8.9% compared to the second quarter of 2025. Collective accommodation — a category that includes youth hostels and group accommodation — totaled 1.3 million nights, an increase of 3.2%. Campsites stood at 1.6 million, recording growth ## Analysis: what the progression means for the Swiss economy
The figure of +0.4% on an annual basis should be read in perspective. The second quarter represents only part of the picture: the first half of the year as a whole closed at -3.1%, with 8.2 million overnight stays compared to about 8.46 million in the same period of 2025. The six-monthly decline is driven by the holiday home sector, which alone loses 360,000 nights compared to the previous year (-8.9%).
### Countertrend Funds Campsites and collective accommodation represent the most dynamic segments. Campsites registered +4.7% in the quarter and +4.4% in the semester, a sign of demand oriented towards low-cost outdoor solutions — consistent with the pressure on the cost of living that continues to characterise 2026. Collective accommodation (hostels, groups) grew by 3.2% quarterly and 1.0% semi-annually, confirming the recovery of school tourism and organized groups after the difficulties of previous years.

## In a nutshell - Repower cuts electricity prices in its grey area - A family of 4 will pay CHF 1,449 in 2027, CHF 20 less - From 2027 differentiated energy rates per season - New Optima voluntary rate with green/yellow/red time slots
## Key facts - **What**: Slight drop in the price of electricity for domestic utilities and introduction of seasonal tariffs - When: News will start from 2027; today's communication from Repower - Where: Network area of the Repower group, mainly in Graubünden - Who: Repower, an energy group based in Poschiavo (GR) - Amount: CHF 1,449 per year for a family of 4 with consumption of 4,500 kWh (-20 CHF, -1.4%) - New: Grischunpower product with more expensive rates in winter and cheaper in summer, average annual energy price unchanged - New product: Optima, hourly variable rate with three levels (green/yellow/red) - Network investments: CHF 30-40 million per year for upgrades and smart grids
Repower, the energy group based in Poschiavo, will slightly reduce electricity prices for domestic utilities in its network area in Graubünden. The announcement came today from the company: in 2027 a family of four with an annual consumption of 4,500 kilowatt hours will pay 1,449 francs of electricity, twenty francs less than the current year. The percentage change is -1.4%.
The ## What's changing for families in Graubünden The reduction of twenty francs per year on a standard consumption of 4,500 kWh is contained — equal to 1.4% — but comes at a time when the cost of living and energy bills remain a sensitive item in the domestic budget throughout Switzerland. For a typical household, the savings amount to about 1.67 francs per month, a figure that alone does not change the structure of spending, but adds to other signs of moderation in energy prices.
It is important to underline a technical detail: the savings indicated refer to Repower's standard Grischunpower supply and do not include municipal taxes. In Graubünden — as in the rest of Switzerland — the final electricity bill consists of the sum of energy, network use, taxes and VAT. The increase in real consumption, a change of category (for example, a change to the Optima tariff) or an increase decided by the individual municipalities can easily cancel or exceed the twenty francs of savings indicated.
### Seasonal Differentiation: Opportunity and Attention The logic of the differentiated tariff is well known: shifting consumption in the summer months, when hydroelectric and solar production is more abundant, is in the best interest of both the customer and the grid. Repower explains this by recalling the greater availability of renewable energy in the summer and the trend of the electricity markets.
For a Grisonese family, the practical question becomes: when is it best to move loads?
